quote: A full agonist occupies all receptors for 100% of the response; a partial agonist occupies, for example, 70% and gives 70%. It introduced affinity and full versus partial agonists but could not explain how all drugs work.
source: Slide ~28 (L01.md): "Full agonist & Partial agonist ≠ Affinity". Transcript 9/22: "between 1% and 99% is your partial" and "it did not explain how all the drugs work". 9/30 review: "C and E, right? They're both producing the same effect ... However, C has a great affinity than E does" (two partials with the same plateau and different affinity, so the plateau is efficacy, Y axis, not occupancy). The question's own reading says the same: "failure to produce a maximal response is not due to decreased affinity". The teach states the occupancy explanation as the rule, which contradicts the review method (affinity = X axis, efficacy = Y axis).
fix: A partial agonist has positive efficacy but less than a full agonist: intrinsic activity between 1% and 99%, so it plateaus below 100% at every dose. The occupancy theory tried to explain this by occupancy alone and could not explain how all drugs work; by his method the plateau (Emax) is efficacy, the left–right position is affinity.

quote: Curve A is a full agonist and curve B is a partial agonist at the same receptor. Under the occupancy theory, why does curve B stop at 70% of the maximal response?
source: Transcript 9/22: "I don't expect you to know or answer to me on the exam who Clark was or Aryans or Stevenson Frescott and Nixon. They're important historical figures in pharmacology, but not for exams." Slide ~28: "FYI: Two Names * Don't NTK, only background info". The stem keys the occupancy theory itself.
fix: Curve A is a full agonist and curve B is a partial agonist at the same receptor. Why does curve B stop at 70% of the maximal response? — key: 'It has lower efficacy (intrinsic activity between 1% and 99%)' [source: transcript 9/22 "between 1% and 99% is your partial"; 9/30 "efficacy ... Up and down"]; distractors: 'It has lower affinity, so it occupies fewer receptors' (why: slide ~28 "Full agonist & Partial agonist ≠ Affinity"; affinity is the X axis), 'It shifts receptors to inactive' (unchanged), 'It has zero intrinsic activity' (unchanged).

quote: Curve C plateaus at 70%: it produces only a percentage of the maximal response, which by the occupancy theory is a partial agonist that occupies only part of the receptors.
source: Same as L01-019: slide ~28 "Full agonist & Partial agonist ≠ Affinity"; 9/30 "efficacy ... Up and down"; 9/28 "All those are partial agonists because they are above 1 and they less than 99". Occupancy is not his rule for reading the plateau.
fix: Curve C plateaus at 70%: it produces only a percentage of the maximal response, so its efficacy is between 1% and 99%, a partial agonist.

quote: a partial agonist produces a percentage of it, for example 70%, because under the occupancy theory it occupies only that fraction of the receptors.
source: As above (slide ~28; 9/28; 9/30). The second sentence of the teach (read the plateau, not the position) is his method; the occupancy clause contradicts it.
fix: A full agonist produces 100% of the response; a partial agonist produces a percentage of it, for example 70%, because its efficacy is between 1% and 99%. Read the plateau, not the position: any curve that reaches 100% is a full agonist, and the one that stops short is the partial.

quote: Antagonists block receptors; they are not described as changing other drugs’ potency.
source: Transcript 9/28: "is the Claritin helping or making the life of histamine more difficult? ... It's gonna be moved to the right." 9/30 review page 5: "Shift? ↓Potency = ↑ED50" for the irreversible antagonist. Antagonists do change an agonist's potency (shift right), so this why is wrong by his own method; the real discriminator is the stem's "does not always act by itself".
fix: An irreversible antagonist acts by itself at the receptor (covalent bond) and makes an agonist less potent and lowers its Emax; it is not the class he calls the magic of pharmacology that can also make other drugs much better.

quote: There are about 7 distinct ones
source: Slide ~39 (not lectured 9/22): "~232 distinct ion channels". Transcript 9/22: "I'm not a person that is gonna ask you a question exam that was on slide 200 at the bottom of the slide on the smallest font possible". The option tests the count 232.
fix: They are intracellular receptors like the steroid hormone receptors (why: 'Ion channels are transmembrane proteins on the cell membrane; intracellular receptors are a separate class.')

quote: expressed in all cells, about 232 distinct types.
source: Same as above; the number is slide-bottom trivia.
fix: Ion channels are transmembrane proteins expressed in all cells. They are classified by the ion they conduct and by what opens them (ligand, voltage or stretch), and they signal by changing membrane potential or ionic composition (Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cl−), because the lipid bilayer is impermeable to ions.
